html:
Description

In peripheral sensory neurons PGE2 released during joint inflammation binds the EP4 receptor, a Gs-coupled GPCR that activates adenylate cyclase and raises cAMP, driving PKA-dependent sensitisation of nociceptor channels such as TRPV1 and NaV1.8. In osteoarthritis models and in human and canine OA, EP4 on peripheral nerve is a principal route by which subchondral and synovial PGE2 produces pain, and EP4 antagonism reduces OA pain. EP4 also drives cartilage matrix catabolism, so it links structural disease and pain.

Colour

Proteins and metabolites are coloured by their contribution to pain: red for those that raise it (they excite or sensitise nociceptive neurons, or drive the inflammation that does), blue for those that relieve it, and olive for the shared signalling machinery (G proteins, RGS, adenylate cyclase, phospholipases, kinases, adaptors, second messengers, ions and nucleotides), whose effect is set by the receptor upstream. Drugs are yellow and classes of molecules white. Each molecule is coloured by its role in this block, so the same molecule can be red in one block and blue in another.

PGE2 and EP4 are red: EP4 raises cAMP in nociceptors and sensitises them. For inflammation the same receptor acts the other way in macrophages, where PGE2 through EP4 suppresses chemokine production (Takayama 2002). Pain is the endpoint of this map, so the colour follows the action on the nociceptor.
